name: Amoxicillin

fields.mechanism_of_action: Amoxicillin is a semisynthetic penicillin-class antibacterial (an analog of ampicillin). It is similar to penicillin in its bactericidal action against susceptible bacteria during the stage of active multiplication, acting through inhibition of cell wall biosynthesis that leads to the death of the bacteria. Resistance to amoxicillin is mediated primarily through beta-lactamase enzymes that cleave the beta-lactam ring, rendering it inactive (FDA label, Amoxicillin tablets, for oral suspension, chewable tablets and capsules (Teva/Northwind Health Company), sections 11 DESCRIPTION and 12.4 MICROBIOLOGY, Mechanism of Action and Resistance). Amoxicillin is stable in the presence of gastric acid and is rapidly absorbed after oral administration (section 12.3 Pharmacokinetics).
indications: Upper respiratory tract infections of the ear, nose and throat caused by susceptible (only beta-lactamase-negative) isolates of Streptococcus species (alpha- and beta-haemolytic isolates only), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus spp. or Haemophilus influenzae (FDA amoxicillin label, section 1.1)

Infections of the genitourinary tract caused by susceptible (only beta-lactamase-negative) isolates of Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis or Enterococcus faecalis (FDA amoxicillin label, section 1.2)

Infections of the skin and skin structure caused by susceptible (only beta-lactamase-negative) isolates of Streptococcus spp. (alpha- and beta-haemolytic isolates only), Staphylococcus spp. or E. coli (FDA amoxicillin label, section 1.3)

Infections of the lower respiratory tract caused by susceptible (only beta-lactamase-negative) isolates of Streptococcus spp. (alpha- and beta-haemolytic isolates only), S. pneumoniae, Staphylococcus spp. or H. influenzae (FDA amoxicillin label, section 1.4)

Adult patients only: Helicobacter pylori infection and duodenal ulcer disease, as triple therapy with clarithromycin and lansoprazole, or dual therapy with lansoprazole delayed-release capsules in patients allergic/intolerant to clarithromycin or with suspected or known clarithromycin resistance (FDA amoxicillin label, section 1.5)

WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 24th list (2025), section 5.1.6.1: amoxicillin is first choice for acute bacterial meningitis and second choice for community-acquired pneumonia (mild to moderate), complicated severe acute malnutrition, exacerbations of COPD, otitis media, pharyngitis, progressive apical dental abscess, sepsis in neonates and children, sinusitis and uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition

Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023, section 7.2.1.2: amoxicillin for treatment of shigellosis and community-acquired pneumonia; also pharyngitis, sinusitis and otitis media; as an alternative to benzathine penicillin in rheumatic fever prophylaxis; and for prophylaxis of infective endocarditis before dental procedures; not for use at community level - CHVs to refer to level 2
contraindications: History of a serious hypersensitivity reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) to amoxicillin or to other beta-lactam antibacterials such as penicillins or cephalosporins (FDA amoxicillin label, section 4 CONTRAINDICATIONS)
side_effects: Most common adverse reactions (>1%) in clinical trials of amoxicillin capsules, tablets or oral suspension: diarrhoea, rash, vomiting and nausea (FDA amoxicillin label, section 6.1 Clinical Trials Experience)

Triple therapy (amoxicillin/clarithromycin/lansoprazole): most frequently reported adverse events were diarrhoea (7%), headache (6%) and taste perversion (5%); dual therapy (amoxicillin/lansoprazole): diarrhoea (8%) and headache (7%) (section 6.1)

Gastrointestinal (post-marketing): drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES), black hairy tongue, and haemorrhagic/pseudomembranous colitis; onset of pseudomembranous colitis symptoms may occur during or after antibacterial treatment (section 6.2)

Immune (post-marketing): hypersensitivity reactions, anaphylactic/anaphylactoid reactions including shock, angioedema, serum sickness-like reactions (urticaria or skin rash with arthritis, arthralgia, myalgia and frequently fever) and hypersensitivity vasculitis (section 6.2)

Skin (post-marketing): rashes, pruritus, urticaria, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, exfoliative dermatitis and linear IgA bullous dermatosis (section 6.2)
Hepatic (post-marketing): a moderate rise in AST and/or ALT (significance unknown); hepatic dysfunction including cholestatic jaundice, hepatic cholestasis and acute cytolytic hepatitis (section 6.2)

Haematological (post-marketing): anaemia including haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenic purpura, eosinophilia, leukopenia and agranulocytosis, usually reversible on discontinuation (section 6.2)
Central nervous system (post-marketing): reversible hyperactivity, agitation, anxiety, insomnia, confusion, convulsions, behavioural changes, aseptic meningitis and/or dizziness (section 6.2)

Miscellaneous (post-marketing): tooth discoloration (brown, yellow or grey staining), most reports in paediatric patients; discoloration was reduced or eliminated with brushing or dental cleaning in most cases (section 6.2)

dosage.adult: Adults and paediatric patients 3 months (12 weeks) and older and weighing more than 40 kg: ear/nose/throat, skin/skin structure and genitourinary tract infections - mild/moderate 500 mg every 12 hours or 250 mg every 8 hours; severe 875 mg every 12 hours or 500 mg every 8 hours. Lower respiratory tract infections (mild/moderate or severe) 875 mg every 12 hours or 500 mg every 8 hours. Overall adult range 750 to 1750 mg/day in divided doses every 8 to 12 hours (FDA amoxicillin label, sections 2.2 and Table 1). H. pylori: triple therapy 1 g amoxicillin with 500 mg clarithromycin and 30 mg lansoprazole twice daily for 14 days; dual therapy 1 g amoxicillin with 30 mg lansoprazole three times daily for 14 days (section 2.4). Treatment should be continued for a minimum of 48 to 72 hours beyond the time that the patient becomes asymptomatic or evidence of bacterial eradication is obtained, and at least 10 days is recommended for any infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes to prevent acute rheumatic fever (section 2.2).
dosage.geriatric: Analysis of clinical studies did not identify differences in responses between elderly (65 and over) and younger patients, but greater sensitivity of some older individuals cannot be ruled out; because amoxicillin is substantially excreted by the kidney and elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function, care should be taken in dose selection and it may be useful to monitor renal function (FDA amoxicillin label, section 8.5 Geriatric Use).
dosage.paediatric: Paediatric patients 3 months (12 weeks) and older and weighing less than 40 kg: ear/nose/throat, skin/skin structure and genitourinary tract infections - mild/moderate 25 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 12 hours or 20 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 8 hours; severe 45 mg/kg/day every 12 hours or 40 mg/kg/day every 8 hours. Lower respiratory tract infections (mild/moderate or severe) 45 mg/kg/day every 12 hours or 40 mg/kg/day every 8 hours (FDA amoxicillin label, section 2.2, Table 1). Neonates and infants aged 3 months (12 weeks) or younger: the recommended upper dose is 30 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours because of incompletely developed renal function; there are currently no dosing recommendations for paediatric patients with impaired renal function (section 2.3). Safety and effectiveness for the treatment of H. pylori infection have not been established in paediatric patients (section 8.4).

interactions: Probenecid: decreases renal tubular secretion of amoxicillin, so concurrent use may result in increased and prolonged blood levels of amoxicillin; co-administration is not recommended (FDA amoxicillin label, sections 7 and 7.1)
Oral anticoagulants: abnormal prolongation of prothrombin time (increased INR) has been reported; monitor and adjust the anticoagulant dose if necessary (section 7.2)
Allopurinol: concurrent administration increases the incidence of rash compared with amoxicillin alone (section 7.3)
Oral contraceptives: amoxicillin may affect intestinal flora, leading to lower oestrogen reabsorption and reduced efficacy of combined oral oestrogen/progesterone contraceptives (section 7.4)

Other antibacterials: chloramphenicol, macrolides, sulfonamides and tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal effects of penicillin in vitro; the clinical significance is not well documented (section 7.5)

Laboratory test interference: high urine concentrations of ampicillin may cause false-positive glucose results with CLINITEST, Benedict's solution or Fehling's solution; enzymatic glucose oxidase tests (such as CLINISTIX) are recommended. A transient decrease in plasma concentration of total conjugated estriol, estriol-glucuronide, conjugated estrone and estradiol has been noted following administration of ampicillin or amoxicillin to pregnant women (section 7.6)
fields.monitoring: The label contains no formal monitoring section; the following monitoring points are stated in the label: monitor closely for skin rash and discontinue amoxicillin if lesions progress, because it may cause severe cutaneous adverse reactions including SJS, TEN, DRESS and AGEP (FDA amoxicillin label, section 5.2); evaluate any patient who develops diarrhoea for Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea, which has been reported over 2 months after antibacterial use, and institute appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibacterial treatment of C. difficile and surgical evaluation as clinically indicated (section 5.4); and monitor renal function in elderly patients and adjust dose in severe renal impairment (sections 8.5 and 8.6). Baseline and follow-up blood counts are not specified in the label.
fields.patient_counselling: Amoxicillin tablets, for oral suspension, chewable tablets and capsules may be taken every 8 hours or every 12 hours depending on the dose prescribed (FDA amoxicillin label, section 17 Patient Counseling Information). Counsel patients that amoxicillin contains a penicillin class drug product that can cause allergic reactions in some individuals. Advise patients about the signs and symptoms of serious skin manifestations and instruct them to stop taking amoxicillin immediately and promptly report the first signs or symptoms of skin rash, mucosal lesions or any other sign of hypersensitivity (section 17). Counsel that diarrhoea is a common problem caused by antibacterial drugs which usually ends when the antibacterial is discontinued, and that watery and bloody stools with or without stomach cramps and fever can occur even as late as 2 or more months after the last dose, in which case the physician should be contacted as soon as possible (section 17). Counsel that antibacterial drugs should only be used to treat or prevent bacterial infections and do not treat viral infections such as the common cold, and that skipping doses or not completing the full course may reduce effectiveness and increase the likelihood of resistance (section 17). It is preferable to refrigerate amoxicillin suspension but not required; shake the suspension well before each use, keep the bottle tightly closed, use a calibrated oral syringe for children and rinse it after each use, and discard any unused portion after 14 days (section 17).
warnings: Anaphylactic reactions: serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions have been reported on penicillin therapy including amoxicillin; although anaphylaxis is more frequent following parenteral therapy, it has occurred with oral penicillins; discontinue amoxicillin and institute appropriate therapy if a reaction occurs (FDA amoxicillin label, section 5.1)

Severe cutaneous adverse reactions: amoxicillin may cause SJS, TEN, DRESS and AGEP; if patients develop skin rash they should be monitored closely and amoxicillin discontinued if lesions progress (section 5.2)

Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES): a non-IgE mediated hypersensitivity reaction characterised by protracted vomiting 1 to 4 hours after ingestion without skin or respiratory symptoms, most cases in patients 18 years of age or younger, with pallor, lethargy, hypotension, shock, diarrhoea within 24 hours and leukocytosis with neutrophilia; discontinue amoxicillin and institute appropriate therapy (section 5.3)

Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea (CDAD): has been reported with use of nearly all antibacterial agents and may range from mild diarrhoea to fatal colitis; consider CDAD in all patients presenting with diarrhoea following antibacterial use, including up to 2 months after treatment (section 5.4)

Development of drug-resistant bacteria: prescribing amoxicillin in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to provide benefit and increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria (section 5.5)

Skin rash in patients with mononucleosis: a high percentage of patients with mononucleosis who receive amoxicillin develop an erythematous skin rash, so amoxicillin should not be administered to patients with mononucleosis (section 5.6)
precautions: To minimize the potential for gastrointestinal intolerance, amoxicillin should be taken at the start of a meal (FDA amoxicillin label, section 2.1 Important Administration Instructions)
Dose reduction is required in patients with severe renal impairment (GFR less than 30 mL/min); such patients should not receive the 875 mg dose (sections 2 and 2.5)
In patients with impaired renal function a reduction in dose is not generally required unless the impairment is severe (section 2.5)

Because of incompletely developed renal function in neonates and young infants, elimination of amoxicillin may be delayed and dosing should be modified in patients 12 weeks (3 months) or younger (section 8.4)

Use of oral suspension: prepare the suspension at the time of dispensing with the stated amount of water, shake well before use, keep the bottle tightly closed, and discard any unused portion after 14 days (section 2.6 and section 17)
serious_adverse_reactions: Anaphylactic reactions, serious and occasionally fatal (FDA amoxicillin label, section 5.1)
Severe cutaneous adverse reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (section 5.2)
Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea, ranging from mild diarrhoea to fatal colitis (section 5.4)
Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES), which may be associated with pallor, lethargy, hypotension and shock (section 5.3)
Interstitial nephritis resulting in oliguric renal failure and crystalluria leading to renal failure after overdose (section 10 Overdosage)
Hepatic dysfunction including cholestatic jaundice, hepatic cholestasis and acute cytolytic hepatitis (section 6.2)
Tooth discoloration (brown, yellow or grey staining), most reports in paediatric patients (section 6.2)
food_interactions: Amoxicillin should be taken at the start of a meal to minimize potential gastrointestinal intolerance (FDA amoxicillin label, section 2.1)

The effect of food on absorption of amoxicillin from the tablets and suspension has been partially investigated; the 400 mg and 875 mg formulations have been studied only when administered at the start of a light meal (section 12.3 Pharmacokinetics, Absorption)
fields.pregnancy_guidance: Reproduction studies in mice and rats at doses up to 2000 mg/kg (3 and 6 times the 3 g human dose based on body surface area) revealed no evidence of harm to the fetus due to amoxicillin. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; because animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, amoxicillin should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed (FDA amoxicillin label, section 8.1 Pregnancy). It is not known whether use of amoxicillin in humans during labor or delivery has immediate or delayed adverse effects on the fetus, prolongs the duration of labor, or increases the likelihood of the necessity for an obstetrical intervention (section 8.2). The label states no lettered FDA pregnancy category (Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule era labelling).
fields.lactation_guidance: Penicillins have been shown to be excreted in human milk. Amoxicillin use by nursing mothers may lead to sensitization of infants, so caution should be exercised when amoxicillin is administered to a nursing woman (FDA amoxicillin label, section 8.3 Nursing Mothers).
fields.overdose: In case of overdosage, discontinue amoxicillin, treat symptomatically and institute supportive measures as required. A prospective study of 51 paediatric patients at a poison control center suggested that overdosages of less than 250 mg/kg are not associated with significant clinical symptoms. Interstitial nephritis resulting in oliguric renal failure has been reported in a small number of patients after overdosage; crystalluria, in some cases leading to renal failure, has also been reported in adults and paediatric patients, so adequate fluid intake and diuresis should be maintained to reduce the risk of crystalluria. Renal impairment appears to be reversible with cessation of drug administration, high blood levels occur more readily in patients with impaired renal function, and amoxicillin may be removed from circulation by hemodialysis (FDA amoxicillin label, section 10 Overdosage).
fields.pharmacokinetics: Absorption: amoxicillin is stable in the presence of gastric acid and is rapidly absorbed after oral administration; 250 mg and 500 mg capsules give peak blood levels 1 to 2 hours after administration in the range of 3.5-5.0 mcg/mL and 5.5-7.5 mcg/mL respectively. Distribution: amoxicillin diffuses readily into most body tissues and fluids, except brain and spinal fluid unless the meninges are inflamed; in serum it is approximately 20% protein-bound, and therapeutic levels were found in interstitial fluid following a 1 g dose. Metabolism and excretion: the half-life of amoxicillin is 61.3 minutes; approximately 60% of an orally administered dose is excreted unchanged in the urine within 6 to 8 hours, and detectable serum levels are observed up to 8 hours after a dose (FDA amoxicillin label, section 12.3 Pharmacokinetics).
clinical_pearls: Amoxicillin should not be given to patients with infectious mononucleosis because a high percentage develop an erythematous rash (FDA amoxicillin label, section 5.6); this is a well-recognised distinguishing feature from ampicillin

Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES) is a non-IgE mediated reaction that can present as protracted vomiting 1 to 4 hours after a dose without rash or respiratory symptoms, predominantly in patients aged 18 or younger; stop the drug immediately (section 5.3)
Amoxicillin is a substrate of renal tubular secretion and is therefore blocked by probenecid (section 7.1)
Amoxicillin covers only beta-lactamase-negative isolates; for beta-lactamase-producing organisms, amoxicillin/clavulanate is required (section 1 and section 12.4)

Severe renal impairment requires dose reduction: GFR 10-30 mL/min 500 mg or 250 mg every 12 hours; GFR less than 10 mL/min 500 mg or 250 mg every 24 hours; hemodialysis 500 mg or 250 mg every 24 hours with an additional dose during and at the end of dialysis (section 2.5, Table 2)
H. pylori treatment is a 14-day combination regimen; eradication has been shown to reduce the risk of duodenal ulcer recurrence (sections 1.5, 2.4 and 14.1)
Amoxicillin oral products carry no boxed warning in the FDA labelling used here; the anaphylaxis risk is managed under Warnings and Precautions (section 5.1)

Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023 classifies amoxicillin in the WHO AWaRe 'Access' group and restricts use at community level, with community health workers referring to level 2 (KEML 2023, sections 7.2.1.2 footnote 93 and Appendix 7)
fields.renal_dose_adjustment: Patients with impaired renal function do not generally require a dose reduction unless the impairment is severe; patients with GFR less than 30 mL/min should not receive the 875 mg dose. Dosing in severe renal impairment: GFR 10 to 30 mL/min, 500 mg or 250 mg every 12 hours depending on severity of infection; GFR less than 10 mL/min, 500 mg or 250 mg every 24 hours; hemodialysis, 500 mg or 250 mg every 24 hours, with an additional dose both during and at the end of dialysis (FDA amoxicillin label, sections 2.5 and Table 2, and section 8.6).
fields.administration_instructions: Oral administration. To minimize gastrointestinal intolerance, take at the start of a meal (FDA amoxicillin label, section 2.1). Tablets, chewable tablets and capsules are taken every 8 hours or every 12 hours depending on the dose prescribed; oral suspension must be shaken well before each use, kept tightly closed, dosed with a calibrated oral syringe for children and discarded after 14 days (section 17). To prepare oral suspension, tap the bottle until all powder flows freely, add approximately one third of the required water, shake vigorously to wet the powder, add the remaining water and shake vigorously again; reconstituted suspension may be given directly on the child's tongue or mixed with formula, milk, fruit juice, water, ginger ale or cold drinks and taken immediately (section 2.6). Store at 20 to 25 degrees C (68 to 77 degrees F) [USP Controlled Room Temperature] and dispense in a tight, light-resistant container with a child-resistant closure (section 16).

notes: The table stores this agent as 'Amoxicillin' with brand_names ['amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium'], which is the combination product rather than amoxicillin alone; the brand list has been corrected to the verified brand product Amoxil. The clinical content is taken from the FDA prescribing information for amoxicillin tablets, capsules, chewable tablets and oral suspension (Teva Pharmaceuticals, rev. 5/2024, repackaged by Northwind Health Company), supplemented by the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (24th list, 2025) and Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023 for indication, strength and placement context, and by the DailyMed AMOXIL listing for the brand name. This label covers oral amoxicillin only: US injectable amoxicillin product labelling is not included, and the WHO eEML lists a powder for injection (250 mg; 500 mg; 1 g as sodium) for amoxicillin which is not covered by the label used here. The label contains no boxed warning; anaphylaxis is managed under Warnings and Precautions (section 5.1), so black_box_warnings is an empty list rather than null.
